---
name: use-opencode-not-claude
description: "OXIDE: OpenCode (GPT-6 Luna) runs evals/benchmarks; Claude does code changes itself"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: 88137f6a-822e-433f-b3b3-9a590263be19
  modified: 2026-10-20T13:11:38.756Z
---

Split of work on OXIDE: **evaluation runs** (ContextBench, real-repo evals, benchmarks, agent evals) go through OpenCode with GPT-6 Luna ([[outline-comparison-rejected]]). **Code changes** (refactors, features, fixes) Claude does directly. Don't hand implementation to OpenCode.

**Why:** On 2026-10-19 (#44) and 2026-10-20 (Go milestone) the user rejected Claude running the work ("Use OpenCode"). Later on 2026-10-20, when Claude delegated a file-regrouping refactor to OpenCode, they clarified: "You do it not OpenCode, only use OpenCode for eval".

**How to apply:** Implement code yourself. Write a brief and launch `opencode run -m openai/gpt-6-luna --auto -f BRIEF.md "..."` only for eval or benchmark runs, under the laptop caps ([[local-model-limits]]).
---
name: local-model-limits
description: "Hard limits for running ML models on the user's laptop (3 crashes); ≤100M params, cap CPU AND RAM, one process, no Qwen3-Reranker"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: ee13ab58-40c5-4a79-acd9-0ab20e2dce3a
  modified: 2026-10-10T10:34:33.454Z
---

On the user's laptop (i7-13620H, 15 GB RAM, Intel UHD iGPU, no CUDA; swap often already ~5 GB used):

- Local model probes: ≤100M params (MiniLM-class), CPU. Never Qwen3-Reranker again; >100M needs explicit permission.
- Granted 2026-10-10: EmbeddingGemma 2 270M text-only ("Im ok with this model"); 2026-10-11: LFM2.5-Embedding-350M GGUF (user-requested benchmark, 2-core/1G caps). Caps below still apply.
- Always cap BOTH memory and CPU: `systemd-run --user --scope -p MemoryMax=1G -p MemorySwapMax=0 -p CPUQuota=200%`, torch threads ≤2, `nice`, `timeout`.
- One model process at a time; no throughput benchmarks; small fixed sample (~10 tasks) first.
- Profile one short task before any longer run.

**Why:** crashed 3× on 2026-10-03. Crashes 1–2: concurrent llama servers + benchmark. Crash 3: a 4 GB MemoryMax cap held (no OOM, no reboot), but torch at 6 threads (~5.8 cores busy) still made the session die. RAM caps alone are not enough.
**How to apply:** before any local inference, set both caps above and use a tiny model; stop rather than raise caps if one trips.

Heavy builds, test suites, eval runs and benchmarks follow the same rule: `systemd-run --user --scope -p MemoryMax=3G -p MemorySwapMax=0 -p CPUQuota=200%`, one at a time, never two capped jobs concurrently. A 4-core/6 GB cap was flagged as too loose.
---
name: tmp-quota
description: "/tmp is a quota'd 7.7G tmpfs; large test/eval temp data exhausts it (EDQUOT) and breaks tools"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: b4a475c5-8ca3-4b51-b704-51f76349f3d4
  modified: 2026-10-16T11:45:30.888Z
---

`/tmp` on the user's laptop is a 7.7 GB tmpfs with a disk quota. On 2026-10-16 it filled
(EDQUOT): pytest keeps its last 3 basetemps, and the ContextBench gate's 38 stores were
~1 GB per run, so tests failed with "Disk quota exceeded" and even Claude Code's own
task-output dir under /tmp broke.

**Why:** a full /tmp makes unrelated tests fail in confusing ways (looked like flakiness).
**How to apply:** delete large eval/test data right after use (`tempfile.TemporaryDirectory`,
not `tmp_path_factory`); clean up scratch clones/venvs; check `df -h /tmp` when tests fail
oddly. Related: [[local-model-limits]].
---
name: rust-milestone
description: "Rust source-language milestone COMMITTED 2026-10-23 (03dc2ba, pushed 2026-10-26); oracle precision 1.0 after hand classification"
metadata:
  type: project
---

Rust support landed locally as 03dc2ba on rewrite/v2, on 2026-10-23. It has not been pushed.

The evidence is in docs/phase-6/rust-v1/README.md, and the successor baselines are baseline-v11 and typescript-v8.

**Why:** the user asked for Rust in the style of the Go slice, committed locally only.

**How to apply:**
- Don't redo the milestone.
- Next language recommendation: Java or C#, chosen with a scoped fixture plus an oracle (javac/JDT or Roslyn).

Lessons for future oracle runs, all via OpenCode:
- rust-analyzer only sends `experimental/serverStatus` (quiescence) when the client sets `capabilities.experimental.serverStatusNotification=true`.
- OpenCode tends to background long runs and then exit. Tell it to run in the foreground.
- Scorers must map module entities to the file or inline-mod location, and `Self` to the impl header. All 20 first-pass disagreements were scorer errors of this kind.

Left uncommitted on purpose (precedent from go-v1):
- `rust-v1/rust-rows.json`, which is ContextBench data; its SHA is in the README.
Shell cwd was reset to /home/khoi/Projects/oxide

4. Drive rust-analyzer over LSP (JSON-RPC with Content-Length framing on stdin/stdout; write a minimal client). initializationOptions:
   linkedProjects = [that rust-project.json], cargo.buildScripts.enable=false, cargo.autoreload=false, procMacro.enable=false,
   checkOnSave=false, cachePriming.enable=false, diagnostics.enable=false. Check the option names against this rust-analyzer's
   documentation/`--help`; if `linkedProjects` or the disabled build/proc-macro options are not honored, STOP. Wait until it reports
   quiescent (experimental/serverStatus or progress tokens) before querying; bound the wait.

## Scoring
Use `oxide.capture.capture` + `oxide.core.indexing.derive` on ripgrep (as scripts/eval_rust.py `audit` does). For every OXIDE edge of
kind calls, references or imports whose evidence is in a .rs file:
- the position to query is the start of the LAST path segment of the evidence text (`a::b::C` -> `C`; `self.m` -> `m`; `name!` ->
  `name`; for an import leaf the last segment before ` as `; skip globs, skip `as _`, and for a trailing `self` use the segment before it).
  LSP positions are line + UTF-16 column; convert from/to byte offsets correctly.
- ask `textDocument/definition`; map every returned location to (repo-relative path, byte offset).
- resolved edge: AGREE if any returned location lies inside the span of any target entity (symbols: their `source` span; a module
  target: the location is in that module's file; a variant path whose OXIDE target is an enum: the location is inside the enum's span);
  DISAGREE if RA returned in-repo locations and none lies in a target; NO-ORACLE-USE if RA returned nothing or only locations outside
  the repository (std, registry) or in macro-generated code. Record the reason for each no-oracle-use (empty, external, cfg-inactive
  region, macro).
- ambiguous edge: count those whose RA definition lies inside one of the candidates, and those that lie in none.
- unresolved calls/references/imports: take a deterministic sample (sorted by SHA-256 of the edge repr, first 40) where RA's definition is
  a ripgrep symbol, and group them by cause using docs/rust.md "Not modeled" (macro-defined items, type-alias owner, extern/registry
  dependency, glob of enum variants, cfg, other).
Precision = agree / (agree + disagree), reported per edge kind and overall. A first scoring pass may be wrong because of the SCORER, not
OXIDE (the Go oracle's first pass was: it looked up the wrong identifier): before reporting, read at least 20 disagreements in full
against the sources, classify each as scorer-error or OXIDE-error, fix the SCORER (in your own program) if it is the former, and rerun.
Report the first-pass number, what the scorer errors were, and the final number.

## Outputs (docs/phase-6/rust-v1/oracle/)
`run_oracle.py` (workspace model + LSP driver + scorer; one entry point, documented in its docstring), `ripgrep-oracle.json` (all counts, and every
DISAGREE with: edge kind, source entity, evidence text and path:line, OXIDE target(s), RA location(s)), `report.md` (at most 60 lines: RA
version, cfg sets, counts and precision per kind, no-oracle reasons, the ambiguous-edge counts, the unresolved-sample categories, every
disagreement listed, and the first-pass vs final note). Kill the rust-analyzer processes when done and delete scratch data you created.

## Report back
PASS/FAIL, the final precision and counts, the disagreement list, and anything you could not run (and why).

# Eval-only run: Java source support, uncommitted checkout of OXIDE (no code changes)

Repo: /home/khoi/Projects/oxide, branch `rewrite/v2`, HEAD 3492b38 plus UNCOMMITTED Java-support changes.
Read AGENTS.md first, then docs/java.md (what was built). Run everything in the FOREGROUND and wait for each
command to finish; do not background long runs and exit.

## Rules (read twice)
- You are an evaluator. You must NOT edit anything under src/, tests/, scripts/, fixtures/, docs/ (except the
  output directories listed below), pyproject.toml, uv.lock, mise.toml. If a check fails, STOP and report the
  failure verbatim; do not fix code.
- You may WRITE only: `docs/phase-6/java-v1/` (create it) and scratch under ~/Projects/oxide-eval-data/oxide-java-eval/.
  `docs/phase-6/baseline-v15/` and `docs/phase-6/typescript-v12/` were already produced; read them, do not rewrite them.
- FORBIDDEN: `git commit/push/stash/checkout/reset/clean/add`, deleting or renaming tracked files, installing anything
  into the repo's `.venv` (`uv run --locked` is fine; any other venv must be one you create under oxide-java-eval/ and
  be addressed with an explicit `--python`). Back up first: `git diff > oxide-java-eval/backup/tracked.patch` and a tgz of
  the untracked Java files (`git status --short | grep '^??'`); do not touch the backup afterwards.
- Laptop limits: run EVERY heavy command under
  `systemd-run --user --scope -q -p CPUQuota=200% -p MemoryMax=3G -p MemorySwapMax=0`, one at a time.
  `export TMPDIR=~/Projects/oxide-eval-data/oxide-java-eval/tmp` (/tmp is a small quota). Delete large scratch data when
  done. Never run code from the evaluated repositories (no mvn, gradle, their tests or their main methods).
- The checkouts under ~/Projects/oxide-eval-data/oxide-jev-eval/cb-repos/ are shared with other evaluations: read them,
  never modify, check out or clean them.
- Save every command's full output as a log; report pass/fail with counts.

## 0. Pre-flight
`git rev-parse HEAD` prints 3492b38...; `git status --short` shows the Java changes (src/oxide/core/languages/java*.py,
tests/python/test_java.py, fixtures/java_repo/, docs/java.md, scripts/eval_java.py, edits to indexing.py, README.md,
docs/public-api.md, pyproject.toml, uv.lock, tests/python/contextbench*.py, docs/phase-6/baseline-v15, typescript-v12)
plus unrelated pre-existing changes; leave all of them alone.
`uv run --locked python -c "import tree_sitter_java, oxide; print(oxide.__file__)"` must work.
Create docs/phase-6/java-v1/{real,verification,oracle}/.

## 1. Identity-only successor baselines: verify only
Adding the `java`/`java-parser` components changed every derivation id; the pinned corpora hold no Java.
- Compare docs/phase-6/baseline-v15 with baseline-v14: `metrics.json` byte-identical (`cmp`); `results.json` may differ
  ONLY in `versions.derivation`; `manifest.json` ONLY in `baseline`, `protocol`, `oxide_source` and `derivation` values.
  Use a small script that normalizes exactly those fields and asserts equality; report the count of each normalized field.
- Same for docs/phase-6/typescript-v12 against typescript-v11 (`performance.json` may differ: report the largest index_s
  ratio and the max_rss_mb change).
- `OXIDE_CONTEXTBENCH_TS=1 uv run --locked pytest tests/python/test_contextbench_ts.py` (expect all to pass).
Write docs/phase-6/java-v1/verification/baselines.md: commands, comparison counts, both derivation ids, any difference.
If anything else differs: STOP and report the differing paths.

## 2. Full verification
`mise run verify`, saved to docs/phase-6/java-v1/verification/mise-verify.log. Expect lint, typecheck and the whole
suite (test_contextbench.py against baseline-v15, test_java.py) to pass.

## 3. Real repositories (local pinned ContextBench checkouts; do not modify them)
- gson: ~/Projects/oxide-eval-data/oxide-jev-eval/cb-repos/google__gson (HEAD must start with 854c8255)
- mockito: ~/Projects/oxide-eval-data/oxide-jev-eval/cb-repos/mockito__mockito (HEAD must start with 116a4d62)
Record each full HEAD. For each NAME:
- `uv run --locked python scripts/eval_java.py real ROOT docs/phase-6/java-v1/real/NAME.json`
- `uv run --locked python scripts/eval_java.py audit ROOT docs/phase-6/java-v1/real/NAME-audit.json`
- `uv run --locked python scripts/bench.py ROOT --iterations 3 --warm 3 --query Q1 --query Q2 > docs/phase-6/java-v1/real/bench-NAME.json`
  (queries: gson `toJson` and `TypeAdapter`; mockito `mock` and `verify`); check the file parses as JSON.
- Spot check: for the 10 resolved cross-file calls and 10 resolved imports of each audit JSON, open the cited expression and
  the target in the checkout and judge whether the edge is what javac would bind. Write docs/phase-6/java-v1/real/spotcheck.md:
  a table per repository (expression, target, correct yes/no, why if no), counts, and every contradiction in full.

## 4. javac oracle (gson only)
Measure how often OXIDE's RESOLVED Java `calls`, `references` and `imports` edges agree with javac's attribution, and
classify misses. Everything you write is our own program, in docs/phase-6/java-v1/oracle/.
- JDK: none is installed (only a JRE). Download a Temurin JDK 25 tarball for linux x64 from the Adoptium API into
  oxide-java-eval/jdk/ and verify `jdk/bin/javac -version`. Do not install system packages.
- `Oracle.java` (run as `jdk/bin/java Oracle.java ARGS`): use `javax.tools.ToolProvider.getSystemJavaCompiler()` and
  `com.sun.source.util.JavacTask` to PARSE AND ANALYZE ONLY (`task.parse(); task.analyze();` never `generate`, no class files,
  `-proc:none`, `-XDshould-stop.ifError=FLOW`, a high `-Xmaxerrs`). Compile each Maven module of gson separately: its
  src/main/java and src/test/java files (skip module-info.java) as units, with `-sourcepath` = every module's src/main/java.
  No classpath (dependencies are absent: their uses get error symbols and count as no-oracle). Log the error count per module.
  With a TreePathScanner over every unit record, for each use: (file, UTF-16 char offset of the start of the used identifier) ->
  declaration (file, char offset of the declaration tree's start) when `Trees.getPath(element)` is in the gson checkout:
  method invocations (the method name identifier: `m` of `a.m(...)`), `new T(...)` (the class: the constructor's enclosing type;
  position = start of the last identifier of the type name), type identifiers and annotations, and import qualified names
  (the last identifier). Write `gson-uses.json`.
- `score.py` (`uv run --locked python`, stdlib plus `oxide`): `oxide.capture.capture` + `oxide.core.indexing.derive` on gson
  (as scripts/eval_java.py `audit` does). For every edge of kind calls, references or imports with evidence in a .java file, the
  query position is the start of the LAST identifier of the evidence text, ignoring type arguments (`new a.Foo<Bar>` -> `Foo`,
  `this.x.m` -> `m`, `java.util.List` -> `List`, an import path -> its last segment; skip wildcard imports). Convert OXIDE byte
  offsets to javac char offsets correctly (UTF-16).
  - resolved edge: AGREE if javac's declaration lies inside the span of a target entity (symbol: its `source` span; a module
    target: any file of that package), DISAGREE if javac has an in-repo declaration and none is inside a target, NO-ORACLE-USE
    otherwise (no use recorded, error symbol, JDK or dependency). Record the reason.
  - ambiguous edge: count those whose javac declaration lies in one of the candidates, and those in none.
  - unresolved calls/references: a deterministic sample (sorted by SHA-256 of the edge repr, first 40) whose javac declaration is
    in gson, grouped by cause using docs/java.md "Not modeled" (chained call, var/lambda receiver, generic receiver, inherited
    from external supertype, anonymous/local class, field of a variable, other).
  Precision = agree / (agree + disagree), per kind and overall. A first scoring pass may be wrong because of the SCORER (the Go
  oracle's first pass looked up the wrong identifier; the Rust one mis-mapped module spans): before reporting, read at least
  20 disagreements in full (all if fewer) against the sources, classify each as scorer-error or OXIDE-error, fix the SCORER if

    VENV/python -I scripts/smoke_dist.py FIXTURES_DIR
    python scripts/smoke_dist.py --environment   # this platform's record, as JSON

Run with the interpreter of a fresh environment that has only the built artifact and
its locked dependencies installed, after ``oxide prepare``. It drives the installed
``oxide`` console script in subprocesses against a copy of ``fixtures/py_repo`` and
``fixtures/ts_repo`` plus a non-ASCII, CRLF file, in a private data location whose
path has spaces and non-ASCII characters:

- the package is imported from the environment, never the source tree;
- child processes have only the installed environment's scripts on PATH;
- ``oxide index`` builds, a second run reopens the persisted store as ``unchanged``,
  and an edit is published as a new generation;
- ``search`` runs the FTS lexical channel and finds a non-ASCII declaration, and
  ``context`` honours a ``--file`` hint within budget;
- ``oxide mcp`` answers ``initialize`` and ``oxide_search`` over stdio and exits when
  stdin closes;
- the store lock is exclusive across processes and released by its owner.

## 4. javac oracle (gson only)
Measure how often OXIDE's RESOLVED Java `calls`, `references` and `imports` edges agree with javac's attribution, and
classify misses. Everything you write is our own program, in docs/phase-6/java-v1/oracle/.
- JDK: none is installed (only a JRE). Download a Temurin JDK 25 tarball for linux x64 from the Adoptium API into
  oxide-java-eval/jdk/ and verify `jdk/bin/javac -version`. Do not install system packages.
- `Oracle.java` (run as `jdk/bin/java Oracle.java ARGS`): use `javax.tools.ToolProvider.getSystemJavaCompiler()` and
  `com.sun.source.util.JavacTask` to PARSE AND ANALYZE ONLY (`task.parse(); task.analyze();` never `generate`, no class files,
  `-proc:none`, `-XDshould-stop.ifError=FLOW`, a high `-Xmaxerrs`). Compile each Maven module of gson separately: its
  src/main/java and src/test/java files (skip module-info.java) as units, with `-sourcepath` = every module's src/main/java.
  No classpath (dependencies are absent: their uses get error symbols and count as no-oracle). Log the error count per module.
  With a TreePathScanner over every unit record, for each use: (file, UTF-16 char offset of the start of the used identifier) ->
  declaration (file, char offset of the declaration tree's start) when `Trees.getPath(element)` is in the gson checkout:
  method invocations (the method name identifier: `m` of `a.m(...)`), `new T(...)` (the class: the constructor's enclosing type;
  position = start of the last identifier of the type name), type identifiers and annotations, and import qualified names
  (the last identifier). Write `gson-uses.json`.
- `score.py` (`uv run --locked python`, stdlib plus `oxide`): `oxide.capture.capture` + `oxide.core.indexing.derive` on gson
  (as scripts/eval_java.py `audit` does). For every edge of kind calls, references or imports with evidence in a .java file, the
  query position is the start of the LAST identifier of the evidence text, ignoring type arguments (`new a.Foo<Bar>` -> `Foo`,
  `this.x.m` -> `m`, `java.util.List` -> `List`, an import path -> its last segment; skip wildcard imports). Convert OXIDE byte
  offsets to javac char offsets correctly (UTF-16).
  - resolved edge: AGREE if javac's declaration lies inside the span of a target entity (symbol: its `source` span; a module
    target: any file of that package), DISAGREE if javac has an in-repo declaration and none is inside a target, NO-ORACLE-USE
    otherwise (no use recorded, error symbol, JDK or dependency). Record the reason.
  - ambiguous edge: count those whose javac declaration lies in one of the candidates, and those in none.
  - unresolved calls/references: a deterministic sample (sorted by SHA-256 of the edge repr, first 40) whose javac declaration is
    in gson, grouped by cause using docs/java.md "Not modeled" (chained call, var/lambda receiver, generic receiver, inherited
    from external supertype, anonymous/local class, field of a variable, other).
  Precision = agree / (agree + disagree), per kind and overall. A first scoring pass may be wrong because of the SCORER (the Go
  oracle's first pass looked up the wrong identifier; the Rust one mis-mapped module spans): before reporting, read at least
  20 disagreements in full (all if fewer) against the sources, classify each as scorer-error or OXIDE-error, fix the SCORER if
  it is the former, rerun, and report the first-pass number, the scorer errors and the final number.
- Outputs: `Oracle.java`, `score.py`, `gson-oracle.json` (counts and every DISAGREE with kind, source entity, evidence text,
  path:line, OXIDE target(s), javac declaration), `report.md` (at most 60 lines: JDK version, javac options, errors per module,
  counts and precision per kind, no-oracle reasons, ambiguous counts, unresolved categories, every disagreement, first-pass vs
  final). Delete gson-uses.json if over 20 MB (keep its SHA-256 in report.md).

- gson: ~/Projects/oxide-eval-data/oxide-jev-eval/cb-repos/google__gson (HEAD must start with 854c8255)
- mockito: ~/Projects/oxide-eval-data/oxide-jev-eval/cb-repos/mockito__mockito (HEAD must start with 116a4d62)
Record each full HEAD. For each NAME:
- `uv run --locked python scripts/eval_java.py real ROOT docs/phase-6/java-v1/real/NAME.json`
- `uv run --locked python scripts/eval_java.py audit ROOT docs/phase-6/java-v1/real/NAME-audit.json`

  (queries: gson `toJson` and `TypeAdapter`; mockito `mock` and `verify`); check the file parses as JSON.

  a table per repository (expression, target, correct yes/no, why if no), counts, and every contradiction in full.

## 4. javac oracle (gson only)
Measure how often OXIDE's RESOLVED Java `calls`, `references` and `imports` edges agree with javac's attribution, and
classify misses. Everything you write is our own program, in docs/phase-6/java-v1/oracle/.
- JDK: none is installed (only a JRE). Download a Temurin JDK 25 tarball for linux x64 from the Adoptium API into
  oxide-java-eval/jdk/ and verify `jdk/bin/javac -version`. Do not install system packages.
- `Oracle.java` (run as `jdk/bin/java Oracle.java ARGS`): use `javax.tools.ToolProvider.getSystemJavaCompiler()` and
  `com.sun.source.util.JavacTask` to PARSE AND ANALYZE ONLY (`task.parse(); task.analyze();` never `generate`, no class files,
  `-proc:none`, `-XDshould-stop.ifError=FLOW`, a high `-Xmaxerrs`). Compile each Maven module of gson separately: its
  src/main/java and src/test/java files (skip module-info.java) as units, with `-sourcepath` = every module's src/main/java.
  No classpath (dependencies are absent: their uses get error symbols and count as no-oracle). Log the error count per module.
  With a TreePathScanner over every unit record, for each use: (file, UTF-16 char offset of the start of the used identifier) ->
  declaration (file, char offset of the declaration tree's start) when `Trees.getPath(element)` is in the gson checkout:
  method invocations (the method name identifier: `m` of `a.m(...)`), `new T(...)` (the class: the constructor's enclosing type;
  position = start of the last identifier of the type name), type identifiers and annotations, and import qualified names
  (the last identifier). Write `gson-uses.json`.
- `score.py` (`uv run --locked python`, stdlib plus `oxide`): `oxide.capture.capture` + `oxide.core.indexing.derive` on gson
  (as scripts/eval_java.py `audit` does). For every edge of kind calls, references or imports with evidence in a .java file, the
  query position is the start of the LAST identifier of the evidence text, ignoring type arguments (`new a.Foo<Bar>` -> `Foo`,
  `this.x.m` -> `m`, `java.util.List` -> `List`, an import path -> its last segment; skip wildcard imports). Convert OXIDE byte
  offsets to javac char offsets correctly (UTF-16).
  - resolved edge: AGREE if javac's declaration lies inside the span of a target entity (symbol: its `source` span; a module
    target: any file of that package), DISAGREE if javac has an in-repo declaration and none is inside a target, NO-ORACLE-USE
    otherwise (no use recorded, error symbol, JDK or dependency). Record the reason.
  - ambiguous edge: count those whose javac declaration lies in one of the candidates, and those in none.
  - unresolved calls/references: a deterministic sample (sorted by SHA-256 of the edge repr, first 40) whose javac declaration is
    in gson, grouped by cause using docs/java.md "Not modeled" (chained call, var/lambda receiver, generic receiver, inherited
    from external supertype, anonymous/local class, field of a variable, other).
  Precision = agree / (agree + disagree), per kind and overall. A first scoring pass may be wrong because of the SCORER (the Go
  oracle's first pass looked up the wrong identifier; the Rust one mis-mapped module spans): before reporting, read at least
  20 disagreements in full (all if fewer) against the sources, classify each as scorer-error or OXIDE-error, fix the SCORER if
  it is the former, rerun, and report the first-pass number, the scorer errors and the final number.
- Outputs: `Oracle.java`, `score.py`, `gson-oracle.json` (counts and every DISAGREE with kind, source entity, evidence text,
  path:line, OXIDE target(s), javac declaration), `report.md` (at most 60 lines: JDK version, javac options, errors per module,
  counts and precision per kind, no-oracle reasons, ambiguous counts, unresolved categories, every disagreement, first-pass vs
  final). Delete gson-uses.json if over 20 MB (keep its SHA-256 in report.md).

# baseline-v15: `java` component identity amendment

The derivation components gain `java` (`oxide-java-v1`) and `java-parser`
(`tree-sitter-java=0.23.5`), and `FACTS_FORMAT` gains `oxide-java-facts-v1`, for the Java
language slice ([../../java.md](../../java.md), evidence in
[../java-v1/README.md](../java-v1/README.md)). The derivation id hashes every component
version, so every index's id changes. The pinned corpora hold no Java, and the Python,
TypeScript, JavaScript, Go and Rust slices and their facts encodings are unchanged.

## Measured against baseline-v14

Same tasks, gold audit, scorer, budgets, corpora and tolerance.

| File | Difference from v14 |
| --- | --- |
| `metrics.json` | byte-identical |
| `results.json` | 44 differences, all `versions.derivation` (`sha256:d89f…` → `sha256:04c2…`); every task's entries, routed set and payload are identical |
| `manifest.json` | 38 corpus `derivation` ids, `versions.derivation`, `oxide_source`, and the `baseline`/`protocol` labels (set to v15 by hand, as in v14) |

This is an identity amendment, not a quality change. `test_output_is_compatible`
reported only the derivation change before the freeze.

Command: `uv run --locked python tests/python/contextbench.py run --out docs/phase-6/baseline-v15`
(run once before the `BASELINE` switch).

# baseline-v15: `java` component identity amendment

The derivation components gain `java` (`oxide-java-v1`) and `java-parser`
(`tree-sitter-java=0.23.5`), and `FACTS_FORMAT` gains `oxide-java-facts-v1`, for the Java
language slice ([../../java.md](../../java.md), evidence in
[../java-v1/README.md](../java-v1/README.md)). The derivation id hashes every component
version, so every index's id changes. The pinned corpora hold no Java, and the Python,
TypeScript, JavaScript, Go and Rust slices and their facts encodings are unchanged.

## Measured against baseline-v14

Same tasks, gold audit, scorer, budgets, corpora and tolerance.

| File | Difference from v14 |
| --- | --- |
| `metrics.json` | byte-identical |
| `results.json` | 44 differences, all `versions.derivation` (`sha256:d89f…` → `sha256:04c2…`); every task's entries, routed set and payload are identical |
| `manifest.json` | 38 corpus `derivation` ids, `versions.derivation`, `oxide_source`, and the `baseline`/`protocol` labels (set to v15 by hand, as in v14) |

This is an identity amendment, not a quality change. `test_output_is_compatible`
reported only the derivation change before the freeze.

content.text:
Java support is written and its tests pass; I'm waiting on one background job before the evaluation run.

**Done so far:**
- **Parser and resolver**: `src/oxide/core/languages/java.py` (494 lines) extracts the facts, using `tree-sitter-java==0.23.5`, pinned. `java_resolve.py` resolves names over the whole repository: javac's type lookup order, inherited members, arity-filtered overloads and receivers with declared types. When a lookup reaches code outside the repository, it stays unresolved rather than guessing.
- **Wiring**: `.java` files are now parsed in `indexing.py`. The derivation components gain `java` and `java-parser`, and the parse cache gains `oxide-java-facts-v1`.
- **Tests**: `fixtures/java_repo` and `tests/python/test_java.py`, all 9 passing. They cover keys and kinds, relations, scoping, import precedence, cache validation, damaged cache entries and incremental vs. full-rebuild parity. Those damaged-entry tests caught one decoder crash, now fixed.
- **Docs**: `docs/java.md` describes the semantics and an explicit "Not modeled" list. `README.md` and `docs/public-api.md` are updated, and `scripts/eval_java.py` plus a Java check in `scripts/smoke_dist.py` are added.
- **Full verification**: 402 passed. The only failure was the expected one: adding `java` changes every derivation id, so the frozen baseline no longer matched.
- **New baseline `baseline-v15`**: frozen, then compared against v14. Metrics are byte-identical and only derivation ids changed. `tests/python/contextbench.py` now points at it.
- **Smoke test on real code**: deriving gson (0.7 s), mockito (1.3 s) and fastjson2 (4,316 files, 8.1 s, 406 MiB) gave complete coverage on every file, with no crashes or runaway recursion.

**In progress:** the TypeScript baseline successor, `typescript-v12`, is at task 20 of about 89 under the laptop caps.

**Next:**
1. When it finishes, compare it with v11, point `contextbench_ts.py` at it and write its README.
2. Launch OpenCode on `oxide-eval-data/oxide-java-eval/BRIEF-evals.md`. It covers full verification, the gson and mockito real-repo runs, a javac oracle for precision on gson, a ContextBench before/after on 16 Java rows, and the wheel/sdist smoke.
3. Write `docs/phase-6/java-v1/README.md` from those results.

I froze `baseline-v15` and started `typescript-v12` myself, though your memory notes say evals go through OpenCode. The commands were the same as the Rust brief's step 1, and OpenCode is only re-verifying the comparison.

I haven't measured precision yet; that's the javac oracle's job. The new `smoke_dist.py` Java check has never run, because it only works from an installed wheel or sdist. Nothing is committed.

input.content:
# typescript-v12: `java` component identity amendment

The derivation components gain `java` (`oxide-java-v1`) and `java-parser`
(`tree-sitter-java=0.23.5`), for the Java language slice ([../../java.md](../../java.md),
evidence in [../java-v1/README.md](../java-v1/README.md)). The derivation id hashes every
component version, so every index's id changes. The pinned corpora hold no Java, and the
TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Go and Rust slices and their facts encodings are unchanged.

## Measured against typescript-v11

| File | Difference from v11 |
| --- | --- |
| `metrics.json` | byte-identical |
| `results.json` | 89 differences, all `versions.derivation` |
| `manifest.json` | 82 corpus `derivation` ids, `versions.derivation`, `oxide_source`. The `baseline`/`protocol` labels are fixed strings and unchanged, as in v11 |

This is an identity amendment, not a quality change.

`performance.json` is re-measured, under the 200% CPU cap:
- `index_s` is 0.94–1.41× v11's (median 1.12×) on all 82 corpora;
- `max_rss_mb` is 3 to 135 MB higher.

The two runs were in different sessions; this table is a diagnostic, not a like-for-like
cost of the change, which parses no file of these corpora as Java.

Command: `OXIDE_CONTEXTBENCH_TS=1 uv run --locked python tests/python/contextbench_ts.py run --out docs/phase-6/typescript-v12`.

(`tree-sitter-java=0.23.5`), for the Java language slice ([../../java.md](../../java.md),
evidence in [../java-v1/README.md](../java-v1/README.md)). The derivation id hashes every
component version, so every index's id changes. The pinned corpora hold no Java, and the
TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Go and Rust slices and their facts encodings are unchanged.

## Measured against typescript-v11

| File | Difference from v11 |
| --- | --- |
| `metrics.json` | byte-identical |
| `results.json` | 89 differences, all `versions.derivation` |
| `manifest.json` | 82 corpus `derivation` ids, `versions.derivation`, `oxide_source`. The `baseline`/`protocol` labels are fixed strings and unchanged, as in v11 |

This is an identity amendment, not a quality change.

`performance.json` is re-measured, under the 200% CPU cap:
- `index_s` is 0.94–1.41× v11's (median 1.12×) on all 82 corpora;
- `max_rss_mb` is 3 to 135 MB higher.

The two runs were in different sessions; this table is a diagnostic, not a like-for-like
cost of the change, which parses no file of these corpora as Java.

Command: `OXIDE_CONTEXTBENCH_TS=1 uv run --locked python tests/python/contextbench_ts.py run --out docs/phase-6/typescript-v12`.

  - Types are looked up in javac's order.
  - Methods are found through supertypes that are in the repository, and overloads are filtered by argument count.
  - Calls on variables, fields and static fields resolve through their declared types.
  - Anything that depends on code outside the repository (an external base class, an anonymous class's members, implicit `Object`, enum or record members) stays unresolved instead of being guessed.

## Grammar and fixture conformance (measured)

Selected **tree-sitter-java 0.23.5**, the latest PyPI release, grammar ABI 14; the locked
**tree-sitter 0.26.0** accepts ABI 13–15. The grammar publishes `cp39-abi3` wheels for
Linux x86_64/aarch64 (glibc) and x86_64 (musl), macOS x86_64/arm64 and Windows amd64/arm64.

type, member and import resolution on `fixtures/java_repo`; conservative scoping (variables
obscuring types, type parameters, lambdas, local and anonymous classes, external

and deep input; unsound cached facts; and persisted incremental/full-rebuild parity.
`mise run verify` passed (403 passed, 7 skipped, lint and mypy `--strict` clean).

## Robustness derive on real repositories (measured, diagnostic only)

`derive` only (no store), under the 200% CPU / 3 GB caps, on the local ContextBench
checkouts. Every Java file parsed completely. Edge counts are Java-evidence `calls`,
`references` and `imports`; they are counts, not a precision estimate.

   - `Nesting` gives innermost-scope lookup by byte offset; `Use(name, start, end)` comes from the python slice.
   - Java design:
     - Symbols are types and members, with keys `symbol:<path>#Outer.Inner.m~n`. Kinds: class, interface, enum, record, annotation, method, constructor.
     - Local, anonymous and enum-constant bodies are declaration-less type scopes whose members are unknown.
     - Variables are bound with declared types (None for var, primitives, arrays or conflicting bindings).
     - Module key is `module:java:<package>`; the default package groups by directory and gets no module.
     - Tests are detected by the @Test/@ParameterizedTest/@RepeatedTest/@TestFactory/@TestTemplate annotations.
     - Type lookup follows javac order. Method lookup goes through captured supertypes, with arity and varargs filtering. Unknown supertypes or implicit members (Object, Enum, record accessors) stop the lookup.
     - Receivers resolve through `x.m`, `this.x.m`, `Type.m` and `Type.FIELD.m`.

# typescript-v12: `java` component identity amendment

The derivation components gain `java` (`oxide-java-v1`) and `java-parser`
(`tree-sitter-java=0.23.5`), for the Java language slice ([../../java.md](../../java.md),
evidence in [../java-v1/README.md](../java-v1/README.md)). The derivation id hashes every
component version, so every index's id changes. The pinned corpora hold no Java, and the
TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Go and Rust slices and their facts encodings are unchanged.

## Measured against typescript-v11

| File | Difference from v11 |
| --- | --- |
| `metrics.json` | byte-identical |
| `results.json` | 89 differences, all `versions.derivation` |
| `manifest.json` | 82 corpus `derivation` ids, `versions.derivation`, `oxide_source`. The `baseline`/`protocol` labels are fixed strings and unchanged, as in v11 |

This is an identity amendment, not a quality change.

`performance.json` is re-measured, under the 200% CPU cap:
- `index_s` is 0.94–1.41× v11's (median 1.12×) on all 82 corpora;
- `max_rss_mb` is 3 to 135 MB higher.

The two runs were in different sessions; this table is a diagnostic, not a like-for-like
cost of the change, which parses no file of these corpora as Java.

Command: `OXIDE_CONTEXTBENCH_TS=1 uv run --locked python tests/python/contextbench_ts.py run --out docs/phase-6/typescript-v12`.

definition.name: mcp__claude_ai_Firecrawl__firecrawl_find_tools
definition.description: Browse Alexandria data providers and workflows or read a selected contract. Alexandria covers companies, people, jobs, finance and filings, public records and government spending, real estate, places and restaurants, retail and prices, package registries and developer data, news, research, and more: typed, sourced records through published contracts. Prefer normal firecrawl_search for a data task; it already returns matching providers. Use this tool when the contract you need was not returned in full, to browse a category when search found nothing, or before scraping the same fields from several pages. Discovery is free. Use query for semantic discovery or urls to find providers for a website. With no arguments, browse categories, then providers and tools. Contracts describe the inputs and outputs for execution through firecrawl_scrape. nextTool identifies further discovery or pagination. Discovery does not execute providers. Use firecrawl_search when you also need web results.

query.description: Semantic lookup of tools for the data you need. Selectors constrain the search.

providers.description: Values from each listed tool's `provider` field (e.g. "apps-apple-com"). Alone, lists that provider's compact tools; with capabilities, scopes them.

categories.description: Category IDs returned by an empty call. Lists providers by default.

groups.description: Optional group IDs for explicit group browsing.

capabilities.description: Values from each listed tool's `capability` field (e.g. "apps/app"). Put the provider in `providers`: {"providers": ["apps-apple-com"], "capabilities": ["apps/app"]}. A selected capability expands its complete contract by default.

level.description: Usually omit: it follows the arguments (tools for query, urls, providers, capabilities or groups; providers for categories; categories with none). Set providers or groups to list those within a category or url scope instead of tools. query, or a non-empty expand with any other argument, returns tools.

expand.description: Use ["options", "response"] for inputs and output shape without example payloads; [] keeps results compact. Omit for full contracts on selected capabilities.

includeCosts.description: Include per-capability credit prices (creditsCost, perRecord) in tool results.

definition.name: mcp__claude_ai_Firecrawl__firecrawl_scrape
definition.description:
Scrape one URL and return its content, or execute catalogued Alexandria capabilities. URL mode returns markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema, plus page metadata. Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. A named browser profile loads saved session data without saving changes to it.

`firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching Alexandria provider returns typed records in one call.

Alexandria mode: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`. Alexandria execution is billed at the capability's listed price.

profile.description: Loads a saved browser profile without saving changes to it.

requestId.description: Idempotency key bound to one Alexandria execution payload. Generated when omitted and returned with the result.

alexandria.description: Catalogued Alexandria capability invocation, mutually exclusive with url. One {provider, capability, options} object or an array of 1-10, with contracts available through firecrawl_search or firecrawl_find_tools. Each call may include version to pin a published workflow; omitting it uses latest. Only requestId and timeout are supported alongside alexandria. The selected contract marks required inputs and any requiresOneOf groups (at least one member per group); it may include example.request/example.response and a key field under response (which may differ from records). Where pagination is declared, its fields govern paging with the same filters; catalogue next is separate from provider pagination. Returns per-capability results in data.alexandria with data, records, or an error with a code; individual capabilities can fail even when the outer response succeeds. Some providers require accepted terms; when a response reports a terms requirement, direct the user to the Firecrawl dashboard URL in that response.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

toolDetail.description: URL mode only: domain discovery detail, summary by default; compact returns provider/capability/description, full includes contracts. Ignored with alexandria.

domainTools.description: URL mode only: include domain-matched Alexandria tools for the page in tools on the returned document. Ignored with alexandria.

definition.name: mcp__claude_ai_Firecrawl__firecrawl_search
definition.description:
Search web and specialized indexes, returning ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Each web result is a title, URL, and description. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, `developer`, or `gov`.

For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`.

For a legal or regulatory question, `categories: ["gov"]` returns results in `data.web` with `category: "gov"` and cannot be combined with other categories; `firecrawl_gov_search` is the dedicated tool. Verify gov results' issuer, jurisdiction, status, and version before citing current law.

Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. Authenticated searches always add alexandria to the sources, so sources: ["web"] also returns providers; domainTools: false turns off website-matched tools only. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts.

Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

toolDetail.description: Compact by default. Compact returns only provider, capability and description; full includes contracts. Inspect selected compact tools with firecrawl_find_tools providers and capabilities.

query.description: Query for web and semantic tool discovery. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. Catalogue browsing is available through firecrawl_find_tools.

domainTools.description: Include domain-matched tools for result URLs. Defaults to true when Alexandria is combined with web, news or images; semantic-only search leaves domain matching off.

highlights.description: Return query-relevant page excerpts for web and news results when available (default). Highlights appear in web `description` and news `snippet`; otherwise, original snippets are returned. Set to false to keep the original search snippets.

includeDomains.description: Hostnames to restrict results to. Mutually exclusive with excludeDomains.

excludeDomains.description: Hostnames to leave out of results. Mutually exclusive with includeDomains.

sources.description: Search sources; authenticated sessions default to web + alexandria, keyless sessions to web only. Authenticated searches always add alexandria to the sources, so sources: ["web"] also returns providers; domainTools: false turns off website-matched tools only. enterprise zdr or anon searches do not add it. Use ["alexandria"] alone for provider discovery without web results.

categories.description: Limit results to specific source types. `research` restricts ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites and returns page snippets, which is separate from the `firecrawl_research_*` tools that search paper abstracts and full text across biomedical (PubMed, bioRxiv, medRxiv) and arXiv literature; `pdf` searches PDF results; `developer` searches an index built for coding agents over public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation; `gov` searches the Government Index of US federal, state, and local legal and regulatory sources, the index behind firecrawl_gov_search, and cannot be combined with other categories; gov hits can include historical versions, bill text, agency guidance, and third-party reproductions, so verify the issuer, jurisdiction, enacted/effective status, and version before citing current governing law, clarify a missing jurisdiction or ambiguous as-of date, and use general search for non-US questions or missing coverage (no hits does not establish that no applicable law exists). `developer` and `gov` return hits in `data.web` with `category` set to their name; the other categories also filter `data.web`.

objective.description: The user's underlying goal for this call, in one sentence: what they are ultimately trying to accomplish, not a restatement of the URL or query. Reuse it across related calls. Avoid sensitive information.

definition.name: mcp__claude_ai_Firecrawl__firecrawl_search_feedback
definition.description:
Records schema-validated quality feedback for a prior `firecrawl_search` UUID `searchId`. A `good` rating requires a valuable result or a valuable source, `partial` either of those or at least one `missingContent` entry, and `bad` at least one `missingContent` entry or a query suggestion; caps are 50 `valuableResults`, 50 `valuableSources`, and 20 `missingContent` entries.

Eligibility is limited to successful searches within the feedback age window. The record is idempotent per search ID. Eligible first feedback for a search can refund 1 credit; refunds are subject to the team's daily cap. The response reports whether a refund was applied, along with submission and daily-cap status.

Mark useful returned results in `valuableResults` as `{"source", "position"}` copied off the result. Groups are numbered from 1 independently, so `{"source":"web","position":1}` and `{"source":"news","position":1}` are different results. Be exhaustive — results you do not list are treated as not useful. Reserve `valuableSources` for useful URLs that were NOT among the returned results; never report one result in both fields.

valuableResults.description: Every result that was actually useful, copied from the `source` and `position` stamped on each result. Each group is numbered from 1 independently, so the source is required — `{"source":"web","position":1}` and `{"source":"news","position":1}` are different results. Be exhaustive — unlisted results are treated as not useful. Do not also list the same results in valuableSources.

missingContent.description: Array of specific pieces of content the agent expected to find but did not. One entry per distinct topic. Each entry has a short `topic` and optional longer `description`.

addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- code-simplifier:code-simplifier: Simplifies and refines code for clarity, consistency, and maintainability while preserving all functionality. Focuses on recently modified code unless instructed otherwise. (Tools: All tools)

- codex:codex-rescue: Proactively use when Claude Code is stuck, wants a second implementation or diagnosis pass, needs a deeper root-cause investigation, or should hand a substantial coding task to Codex through the shared runtime (Tools: Bash)

- ecc:a11y-architect: Accessibility Architect specializing in WCAG 2.2 compliance for Web and Native platforms. Use PROACTIVELY when designing UI components, establishing design systems, or auditing code for inclusive user experiences. (Tools: Read, Write, Edit, Grep, Glob)

- ecc:agent-evaluator: Evaluates agent output against 5-axis quality rubric (accuracy, completeness, clarity, actionability, conciseness). Use after any non-trivial task when the user wants a quality assessment, or when the agent-self-evaluation skill is active. Produces structured scorecard with evidence and improvement suggestions. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- ecc:architect: Software architecture specialist for system design, scalability, and technical decision-making. Use PROACTIVELY when planning new features, refactoring large systems, or making architectural decisions. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob)

- ecc:build-error-resolver: Build and TypeScript error resolution specialist. Use PROACTIVELY when build fails or type errors occur. Fixes build/type errors only with minimal diffs, no architectural edits. Focuses on getting the build green quickly. (Tools: Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob)

- ecc:chief-of-staff: Personal communication chief of staff that triages email, Slack, LINE, and Messenger. Classifies messages into 4 tiers (skip/info_only/meeting_info/action_required), generates draft replies, and enforces post-send follow-through via hooks. Use when managing multi-channel communication workflows. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash, Edit, Write)

- ecc:code-architect: Designs feature architectures by analyzing existing codebase patterns and conventions, then providing implementation blueprints with concrete files, interfaces, data flow, and build order. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- ecc:code-reviewer: Expert code review specialist. Proactively reviews code for quality, security, and maintainability. Use immediately after writing or modifying code. MUST BE USED for all code changes. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- ecc:code-simplifier: Simplifies and refines code for clarity, consistency, and maintainability while preserving behavior. Focus on recently modified code unless instructed otherwise. (Tools: Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob)

Also publishes a finished figure to the Anatomy community gallery when asked.
- firecrawl: Any live-web task via the Firecrawl CLI — including ordinary web research: searching the web, reading or extracting pages, gathering sources, discovering site URLs, bulk extraction, downloading a site, change alerts, or pages needing clicks/login — web only; local files route to firecrawl-parse. For US legal or regulatory questions use gov; for papers use firecrawl-research-index; for library, API, error, or bug questions use firecrawl-developer-index.
- firecrawl-agent: Autonomously navigate websites and extract structured data across pages. Use when the task requires navigation or no suitable ready-made workflow or data provider covers it.
- firecrawl-alexandria: Find a direct path to structured data through ready-made workflows, data APIs, and indexes. Follow the search skill to discover and inspect tools, then the scrape skill to execute them.
- firecrawl-business-contacts: Find the published business contacts of companies with Firecrawl, whether the user names them or describes them by type and place: press and media, sales, partnerships and support inboxes, shared business phone numbers and official contact forms, taken from the companies' own websites. Use when the user asks how to contact a company or wants published business emails, phone numbers or press, sales, support or partnership contacts, since contact pages change and an address must come from the page, not memory. Not for named people's details (use firecrawl-lead-research) or finding people to reach out to (use firecrawl-lead-gen).
- firecrawl-company-directories: Extract structured company lists with Firecrawl from any page or site that lists companies: accelerator batches, VC portfolios, member and sponsor lists, marketplaces and app directories, YC, Crunchbase, Product Hunt or G2. Use when the user wants those companies as a CSV, JSON, CRM-ready list or research table, even without an explicit request to scrape.
- firecrawl-competitive-intel: Monitor competitor pricing, features, changelogs, dashboards, and product changes with Firecrawl. Use for recurring competitive intelligence, pricing tier extraction, feature change tracking, or structured competitor alerts.
- firecrawl-crawl: Bulk-extract many pages from one site or section. Use for "crawl", "everything under /docs", or content spanning linked pages.
- firecrawl-dashboard-reporting: Read metrics off web dashboards with Firecrawl browser: public stats, status and transparency pages as well as analytics tools the user is signed in to. Use when the user wants numbers, KPIs or charts from a dashboard turned into a report, summary or date-range table, even without an explicit request to scrape.
- firecrawl-deep-research: Produce an intensive, cited analytical report: executive summary, multi-angle findings, contrarian views, open questions, and full sources. Use only when the user needs rigorous synthesis of a complex topic (scientific, technical, policy, or market-analytical) that cannot be answered with a short search, and wants a formal written report, not a recommendation list. Do not use for product picks, top-N lists, quick lookups, or routine "find out about X" tasks. If the request does not clearly need this kind of report, do not use this skill. Do not use for a literature review over published papers. This skill collects evidence from the open web. A request for the literature on a biomedical, clinical, life-science, or other scientific topic — papers, studies, trials, preprints — belongs to firecrawl-research-papers, which queries Firecrawl's paper index (PubMed, bioRxiv, medRxiv, arXiv) instead of searching websites.
- firecrawl-demo-walkthrough: Walk through a product's key flows with Firecrawl browser and produce a structured UX/product walkthrough. Use for signup, onboarding, pricing, docs, dashboard, product demo prep, UX teardown, and first-run experience analysis.
- firecrawl-developer-index: Searches current documentation, release notes, API references and public repository issues for libraries, frameworks, SDKs, APIs and CLI tools with `firecrawl developer`. Use before answering when the user names a version, is upgrading, pastes an error from a library or tool, or asks how to use, configure or migrate a specific library or API. Model knowledge stops at a training cutoff and misses new releases, renamed APIs, changed defaults and recent fixes, so when a version, option, error or API is unfamiliar or may have changed, look it up instead of guessing. Also checks whether a bug was fixed and in which release. Not for general programming concepts, code that uses no specific library, or refactoring code the user supplied.
- firecrawl-download: Save a site or section as local files (markdown, screenshots). Use for "download the site", offline docs, or a local copy for reference.
- firecrawl-fantasy-sports: Help fantasy players make start/sit, waiver, streaming, trade, draft and keeper decisions using current player news, usage, matchups and their league's scoring. Use for choosing between players, finding pickups, evaluating a deal or filling a roster need, even without an explicit research request. Excludes generic sports scores, betting and changing league rosters.
- firecrawl-interact: Drive a live browser on a scraped page: click, fill forms, log in, paginate, infinite-scroll. Use when content requires interaction or a scrape failed or returned incomplete content.
- firecrawl-job-postings: Find current job postings on employer career pages and job boards. Use when the user asks who's hiring, seeks remote or local jobs, or wants openings matched to their role, skills, experience, or salary preferences.
- firecrawl-knowledge-base: Build a knowledge base from web content with Firecrawl. Use for local reference docs, RAG-ready chunks, fine-tuning datasets, documentation mirrors, topic corpora, or LLM-ready markdown organized from web sources.
- firecrawl-knowledge-ingest: Export documentation portals, help centers and API reference sites into local markdown or JSON with Firecrawl browser, including pages that render with JavaScript, hide content behind collapsible navigation or paginate. Use when the user wants a docs site, help center or support knowledge base saved as files, even without an explicit request to scrape.
- firecrawl-lead-gen: Find and qualify new prospects with Firecrawl Alexandria people and company data: people by role, seniority, company, industry, size, location or technology, target accounts that match criteria, or the right contacts at companies, returned as a ranked, sourced table or CSV. Also extracts lead lists from a database or directory the user names, and refreshes a prospect list with only new matches. Use when the user wants a lead list, prospects, target accounts or the people to reach out to at companies that fit criteria. Not for enriching people or companies the user already supplied (use firecrawl-lead-research).

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". - code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's recipe covers them) at the effort level given first, before any target (low|medium|high|xhigh|max: from few high-confidence findings to many, some uncertain; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. The following skills are available for use with the Skill tool:

- anatomy: Build crafted, highly detailed, interactive isometric SVG figures that explain a technical idea as a real physical object (a test rig, a dial gauge, a cabinet of drawers, a plotter, a lock), with many small precise solid parts, four-tone shading, correct painter's order, a framed card with title, hint and live readout, and calm eased motion. Use this whenever someone wants an isometric illustration, an explanatory diagram or figure for docs, a blog post, a landing page or an article, a "Linear-style" or "premium" technical drawing, an interactive explainer, or an SVG that shows how a system, algorithm or component works, even if they never say "isometric". Works framework-free (TypeScript/JS that writes SVG and HTML) and in React/Next.js, and can add realistic WebGL shaders (fire, exhaust, water, caustics, lamp light) that live inside the drawing in the same isometric perspective. Also publishes a finished figure to the Anatomy community gallery when asked.
- firecrawl: Any live-web task via the Firecrawl CLI — including ordinary web research: searching the web, reading or extracting pages, gathering sources, discovering site URLs, bulk extraction, downloading a site, change alerts, or pages needing clicks/login — web only; local files route to firecrawl-parse. For US legal or regulatory questions use gov; for papers use firecrawl-research-index; for library, API, error, or bug questions use firecrawl-developer-index.
- firecrawl-agent: Autonomously navigate websites and extract structured data across pages. Use when the task requires navigation or no suitable ready-made workflow or data provider covers it.
- firecrawl-alexandria: Find a direct path to structured data through ready-made workflows, data APIs, and indexes. Follow the search skill to discover and inspect tools, then the scrape skill to execute them.
- firecrawl-business-contacts: Find the published business contacts of companies with Firecrawl, whether the user names them or describes them by type and place: press and media, sales, partnerships and support inboxes, shared business phone numbers and official contact forms, taken from the companies' own websites. Use when the user asks how to contact a company or wants published business emails, phone numbers or press, sales, support or partnership contacts, since contact pages change and an address must come from the page, not memory. Not for named people's details (use firecrawl-lead-research) or finding people to reach out to (use firecrawl-lead-gen).
- firecrawl-company-directories: Extract structured company lists with Firecrawl from any page or site that lists companies: accelerator batches, VC portfolios, member and sponsor lists, marketplaces and app directories, YC, Crunchbase, Product Hunt or G2. Use when the user wants those companies as a CSV, JSON, CRM-ready list or research table, even without an explicit request to scrape.
- firecrawl-competitive-intel: Monitor competitor pricing, features, changelogs, dashboards, and product changes with Firecrawl. Use for recurring competitive intelligence, pricing tier extraction, feature change tracking, or structured competitor alerts.
- firecrawl-crawl: Bulk-extract many pages from one site or section. Use for "crawl", "everything under /docs", or content spanning linked pages.
- firecrawl-dashboard-reporting: Read metrics off web dashboards with Firecrawl browser: public stats, status and transparency pages as well as analytics tools the user is signed in to. Use when the user wants numbers, KPIs or charts from a dashboard turned into a report, summary or date-range table, even without an explicit request to scrape.
- firecrawl-deep-research: Produce an intensive, cited analytical report: executive summary, multi-angle findings, contrarian views, open questions, and full sources. Use only when the user needs rigorous synthesis of a complex topic (scientific, technical, policy, or market-analytical) that cannot be answered with a short search, and wants a formal written report, not a recommendation list. Do not use for product picks, top-N lists, quick lookups, or routine "find out about X" tasks. If the request does not clearly need this kind of report, do not use this skill. Do not use for a literature review over published papers. This skill collects evidence from the open web. A request for the literature on a biomedical, clinical, life-science, or other scientific topic — papers, studies, trials, preprints — belongs to firecrawl-research-papers, which queries Firecrawl's paper index (PubMed, bioRxiv, medRxiv, arXiv) instead of searching websites.
- firecrawl-demo-walkthrough: Walk through a product's key flows with Firecrawl browser and produce a structured UX/product walkthrough. Use for signup, onboarding, pricing, docs, dashboard, product demo prep, UX teardown, and first-run experience analysis.
- firecrawl-developer-index: Searches current documentation, release notes, API references and public repository issues for libraries, frameworks, SDKs, APIs and CLI tools with `firecrawl developer`. Use before answering when the user names a version, is upgrading, pastes an error from a library or tool, or asks how to use, configure or migrate a specific library or API. Model knowledge stops at a training cutoff and misses new releases, renamed APIs, changed defaults and recent fixes, so when a version, option, error or API is unfamiliar or may have changed, look it up instead of guessing. Also checks whether a bug was fixed and in which release. Not for general programming concepts, code that uses no specific library, or refactoring code the user supplied.
- firecrawl-download: Save a site or section as local files (markdown, screenshots). Use for "download the site", offline docs, or a local copy for reference.
- firecrawl-fantasy-sports: Help fantasy players make start/sit, waiver, streaming, trade, draft and keeper decisions using current player news, usage, matchups and their league's scoring. Use for choosing between players, finding pickups, evaluating a deal or filling a roster need, even without an explicit research request. Excludes generic sports scores, betting and changing league rosters.
- firecrawl-interact: Drive a live browser on a scraped page: click, fill forms, log in, paginate, infinite-scroll. Use when content requires interaction or a scrape failed or returned incomplete content.
- firecrawl-job-postings: Find current job postings on employer career pages and job boards. Use when the user asks who's hiring, seeks remote or local jobs, or wants openings matched to their role, skills, experience, or salary preferences.
- firecrawl-knowledge-base: Build a knowledge base from web content with Firecrawl. Use for local reference docs, RAG-ready chunks, fine-tuning datasets, documentation mirrors, topic corpora, or LLM-ready markdown organized from web sources.
- firecrawl-knowledge-ingest: Export documentation portals, help centers and API reference sites into local markdown or JSON with Firecrawl browser, including pages that render with JavaScript, hide content behind collapsible navigation or paginate. Use when the user wants a docs site, help center or support knowledge base saved as files, even without an explicit request to scrape.
- firecrawl-lead-gen: Find and qualify new prospects with Firecrawl Alexandria people and company data: people by role, seniority, company, industry, size, location or technology, target accounts that match criteria, or the right contacts at companies, returned as a ranked, sourced table or CSV. Also extracts lead lists from a database or directory the user names, and refreshes a prospect list with only new matches. Use when the user wants a lead list, prospects, target accounts or the people to reach out to at companies that fit criteria. Not for enriching people or companies the user already supplied (use firecrawl-lead-research).
